newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda to synchronise model cycle with Ford.
newsitem.headline: Mazda to synchronise model cycle with Ford.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp said on Thursday it has agreed with affiliate Ford Motor Co to synchronise car production cycles and share common platforms in a bid to cut costs at the troubled Japanese carmaker.
Mazda president Henry Wallace, touted as the first foreigner to run a major Japanese company, said the two companies would share a number of car platforms, including engines and transmissions.
Mazda, Japan's fifth-largest carmaker, is one-third owned by Ford.

Their long-standing ties strengthened last year when Wallace, a Ford official seconded to Mazda, took over as Mazda's president, setting himself the task of steering the troubled company back to prosperity.
"I think we have made progress on a wide series of fronts, obviously on product development," Wallace told reporters.

Wallace, 51, said that the pact which was reached at the end of last month on product cycles would allow the two to share basic design work and engineering expertise and to raise product capabilities worldwide.
Mazda will use the expertise it has in small engines and transmissions, passenger and commercial cars, he said.
The platform-sharing, which has long been anticipated, will enable the two companies to cut development costs, as well as costs of car parts through joint procurement in volume, analysts say.
Wallace said that a "substantial" portion of Mazda cars would come under the platform-sharing plan.
But he remained tight-lipped about on any further details such as how many platforms would be shared, for which models, or when the sharing would take place.
Wallace said that under the strategy, Mazda's production will rise.
Industry analysts expect the two to share a common platform for their mainstay cars -- Mazda's Familia and Ford's Escort -- from the year 2002.
Last week, Wallace told Reuters in an interview that the real synergies in terms of a production increase will come beyond the year 2000.
Turning to Mazda's business performance, Wallace said on Thursday that the business is moving in "the right direction".
Mazda is renowned for engineering expertise but has faced a shrinking market share since its strategy of becoming a niche maker of luxury cars and distinctive sports cars fizzled.
Wallace said that the firm's financial structure and sales were improving, but he saw no surprises in its business results for the year to March 1997, due to be announced in late May.

In November, Mazda saw its parent current profit rising to 11 billion yen ($88.0 million) in 1996/97, nine times higher than the year before, when it marked its first profit in three years on sales of securities holdings and painful cost-cutting.
Wallace said the company enjoyed a ries in its domestic market share in the January-March quarter of this year, helped by strong demand ahead of the sales tax increase on April 1.
Wallace attributed the higher market share to continuing success of the new Demio models, launched last year, as well as the favourable effects of the company's advertising.
He added that, given these factors, sales growth momentum will continue. ($1=125 yen)
